steps.prompt: Make a heavy walking mech for a three.js game, about 6 m tall. Two digitigrade legs, an armoured torso that turns at the waist, a cockpit with a glass canopy, a shoulder-mounted missile pod and two heavy arms: a rotary cannon on the right and a claw on the left. Every joint has to be its own named pivot (hip, knee, ankle, toe, waist, shoulder, elbow) so I can drive it from code, and the hydraulic pistons on the legs should really follow the joints. Add one looping Walk clip where the feet plant without sliding and the torso sways and counter-rotates. It should look like it came out of a AAA concept: layered armour plates with panel lines, weathered paint, hazard stripes, exposed cables and machinery at the joints. Keep the GLB under 5 MB so it loads in a browser. Save it when you're happy with it.

Good bones. Three notes from me.

The paint still reads as flat olive with specks on it. I want wear you can believe: chipped paint showing bare metal along plate edges, grime settled into the panel lines, oil and rust streaks running down from the joints and bolts, and lower legs that are darker and dustier than the torso.

The shoulders, forearms and feet are plain boxes and wedges next to the detail on the legs. Give them layered plates, bevelled edges, bolts and vents, and make the feet read as armoured toes with rubber soles.

The cannon barrels and joint machinery should read as real gunmetal, with some sharp highlights.

Keep the height, every joint name, the Walk clip and the 5 MB limit, and save it as a new revision of the same asset.
Swap the left claw for a long rail cannon with glowing coils along the barrel. Keep the Walk clip, every joint name and every other part as they are, and save it as a new revision of the same asset.

final.alt: The finished walking mech in three-quarter view: olive armour with chipped edges and hazard stripes, a rotary cannon on its right arm, a long rail cannon with glowing cyan coils on its left, a glass cockpit and a shoulder missile pod, standing on two digitigrade legs with hydraulic pistons.

paint-before.alt: Close view of the shoulder armour on the first revision: flat olive paint with a few specks.

paint-after.alt: The same shoulder on the second revision: chipped edges down to bare metal, grime in the panel lines, rust streaks, bolts, louvred vents and layered plates.

before.alt: The mech on revision 2, with a three-fingered claw on its left arm.

after.alt: The mech on revision 3 from the same camera, with a long rail cannon and glowing coils in place of the claw.

make-sheet.alt: The agent's six-view contact sheet of the first saved revision: front, right, back, left, top and three-quarter, each with a yellow label.

subjects.name: Gothic cathedral

steps.prompt: Build a massive Gothic cathedral, the kind of model that makes a professional 3D artist stop and look. True scale: about 130 m long with twin west towers about 80 m tall. A nave of nine bays with side aisles, transepts, and an apse ringed with radiating chapels. Flying buttresses with crocketed pinnacles on every bay, and gargoyles along the walls. A west front with three deep portals, robed saints in the door jambs, carved tympana over the doors, a gallery of kings, and a great rose window with real stone tracery. The statues have to read as sculpted figures, not blocks. Stained glass in every window, as real art: the rose and the big windows should depict figures and scenes in leaded panes, not just coloured squares. Use real textured PBR materials: weathered limestone with carved detail in the normals, patinated lead roofs, aged oak doors with iron straps, gilded accents. The inside has to hold up too: clustered columns, triforium, clerestory and ribbed vaults, statues in niches and glass that colours the view. Keep the GLB under 15 MB so it can load in a browser. Build it from parameters so the design can change later. Save it when you're happy with it.

Strong bones. The plan, the vaults and the view down the nave are right, and I believe the scale. As art it isn't there yet, and this has to stop a professional 3D artist. I looked at it from the ground outside, up close at the portals and from inside. My notes, most important first.

The statues look like melted candles. Faces have no real features, hands are mittens, feet are two balls and the heads jam straight into the canopies. The figures in the door arches are thin cut-outs floating on the stone, and the lintel's reliefs are buried so only stray bits poke out. Sculpt them like the real thing at Chartres and Reims: long columnar bodies, deep folds you could put a finger in, real faces with brow, nose, lips, hair and beards, hands that grip what they hold, feet on a carved base and room above the head. Make them different people: a bishop in a mitre, a crowned king, a veiled queen, an apostle with a key, a smiling angel, the Virgin and Child on the central door post. I would rather have fewer figure types that are truly good than many that are poor. Carve the tympana as scenes, with figures that overlap and turn to each other, not a row of people on wallpaper.

The glass looks like clip art: flat primary colours and cartoon people. Real medieval glass is deep ruby and cobalt with no two panes quite alike, black lead lines, and brown painted shading that draws faces, hair and drapery. The rose should be the most beautiful thing in the building. From outside, glass should read dark and deep with the colour only hinting through. Right now the windows are as bright as toys outside, and some wash out to pale pink at an angle. The colour belongs inside.

The stone has no age and no depth. Outside it is one clean cream everywhere, so you can't feel how deep the portals are. This building has stood for 700 years: soot in the recesses, rain streaks under every ledge and sill, each block a slightly different colour, darker and greener toward the ground. The viewer has no cast shadows, so bake the light in: a low sun from one side, so the portals go deep, the galleries go dark behind their columns and every ledge throws a shadow below it. The printed quatrefoil pattern on the portal walls and tympana looks like wallpaper, so carve it or remove it. The tower walls are flat ashlar with thin lines stuck on, so give them real blind arcades and relief. Inside, warm the stone, and let it go darker low in the aisles and lighter up in the vault. The coloured light on the floor looks like painted tiles: make it soft pools with the shape of the windows.

Materials should hold up close: lead roofs with visible sheets, seams and streaked patina instead of stretched noise, stone with tool marks instead of round pockmarks, and gold that looks like gold instead of mustard. The altar's gold box should become a carved retable or go.

Faults I can see. A free-standing column sticks out of the north transept front, between the portal and the big window. The flying buttresses are thick flat boards: make them real arches, thin and pierced, with a sloped top. The bell openings are dark walls with nothing in them: make them real openings with louvres. The arches around the apse look like fangs hanging from above instead of springing from the piers.

Keep the plan, the dimensions and the parameters. Keep the GLB under 15 MB and leave about 1 MB free, because I will want changes later. Textures are only 1.4 MB of the file, so spend your bytes on what gets looked at closely. Save it as a new revision of the same asset.

I'm back, and thanks for the honest report. The nave, the vaults and the rose seen from outside are what I wanted, and the stone finally looks old. Here's what comes next, most important first.

A correction before that. I told you the build limit was 120 seconds, and your kiln_save still failed after about a minute. I don't know why yet, so plan on 60. With this machine quiet, your saved revision builds in 32 seconds, so most of those failures were other jobs on the machine rather than your program. You have more room than you thought.

It has no ground. Apart from a paved patch at the west doors, the building floats. Give it real ground all the way round: worn flagstones for about 20 m, a step or two up to each door, rough grass or packed earth at the edge, and dark grime where the walls meet it. Make the ground its own named part, so it can be taken away if the building is later placed in a town. Keep its top a few centimetres above y = 0, so it doesn't fight with a viewer's ground plane.

The corners aren't real architecture. At the corners of the towers and transepts, thick wall plates stick out past the corner and overlap each other, and high on the towers some hang in the air with a slanted edge. Around the apse and along the sides, the buttresses are huge plain boxes, and the set-offs on the west front's buttresses are thin sheets that stick out like awnings. Build real buttresses: solid piers tied into the wall, narrower as they rise, stepping back in two or three stages, each step a sloped stone cap that belongs to the pier. Where two meet at a corner they should meet cleanly, or run diagonally as one. From any angle, nothing should float, overlap or pass through anything else.

Inside. Fix the light bug you found: the piers on one side are still blue-grey. The shadows on the vaults and piers have hard-edged bands, and the light pools on the floor break into hard-edged islands up close. Make them smooth gradients.

The portals, up close. The canopies over the door statues float far above their heads on thin sticks, like hanging lamps. Bring each one down to just above its head, with the figure standing against its column. The tympanum figures stand on shelves like dolls, in front of a wall of blocks. Carve them out of the stone as relief, with no block joints behind them. The gold frame around Christ is a thin wire with angels passing through it, so make it a carved frame, gilded. The kneeling figures have pumpkin-shaped skirts. From the ground the gallery kings are faceless slivers, so give them bodies and crowns. The queen and the Virgin need different faces. The door straps end in curls that read as the number 3, so make them forged hinges. Remove the yellow blotches like coins at the foot of the portal walls, and the little L-shaped chips scattered around the rose.

The glass. From outside, the windows read as flat purple with red specks. Make them nearly black, with faint lead lines and only a hint of colour, the way the rose already does. Inside, the grounds lean magenta, so keep them ruby and cobalt. The high apse windows have a white ladder across the middle: take it out. I still want the rose to be the most beautiful thing in the building, so look at it from inside and make it so.

The roofs look like a patchwork quilt from above. Make long lead sheets running down the slope, with raised seams and streaks.

Then, if there's room, what your report left open: rain streaks on the apse, chapels and buttress sides, and a shadow under every main ledge.

Keep the plan, the parameters and the height. Keep the GLB under 15 MB and leave at least 1 MB and some build time free, because I'll ask for a change that adds geometry afterwards. Save it as a new revision of the same asset, then tell me plainly what's done and what isn't.
Add two more bays to the nave and raise a lead-covered spire over the crossing, about 100 m to the tip. Leave everything else as it is and save it as a new revision of the same asset.

One fault, from looking inside. The coloured light on the nave floor isn't light. It's painted patches: they lean the wrong way for the sun you baked into the stone, their colours aren't the colours of the glass, and they run straight through the piers as if the piers weren't there.

Make it real, and baked like the rest. Use the same sun as the stone, P.sun, low from the south-west. For each point of the floor, trace back towards the sun. If the ray clears the south arcade without hitting a pier and comes through a south aisle window, the floor takes that window's colour at that height, from its actual panes or a close average of them. Otherwise it takes nothing. So each window throws a long slanted pool that runs north and east across the floor, with the shape of its lancets and tracery softened, and the piers cut clean shadows through it. Keep the edges soft, and keep it subtle enough that the paving still reads through it. If the same rays land on the north piers or walls and you can bake that cheaply, do it. If not, leave it and say so.

Leave everything else as it is: the plan, the height, the stone and the glass. Keep the GLB under 15 MB. You have about 0.3 MB free, so take the budget out of the old patches. Keep the build inside the limit. Save it as a new revision of the same asset, then tell me plainly what's done and what isn't.

I looked at the floor light again and it still isn't right. At this sun it runs the whole way across the nave, past the columns and up the north piers, and your own number says almost none of it could get past the buttresses outside.

Fix it by moving the sun. Set P.sun to about [0.11, 0.79, -0.61]: about 52 degrees up and about 10 degrees west of due south. I tried a few suns on a scratch copy of your source, with the outside counted. With this one each south aisle window lands as its own window-shaped pool that passes between the piers and stops around the middle of the nave, short of the north piers. Further west, the buttresses and piers cut the pools into thin streaks. Adjust it a little if your own checks say so, and tell me if you do.

Count everything in the trace, including the outside: buttresses, flyers, pinnacles, towers and transepts. No light passes through stone. Tell me what share of the rays reaching a window now clear everything.

Start the floor image at the south aisle wall, because light now lands in the aisle, and end it just past where the last light falls, so the texels go where the light is. Where rays stop on a pier, that's now the south faces of the south piers, so put the pier skins there. The north piers should get nothing.

The colour reads as pink and lavender with pale blobs. Make it read as ruby and cobalt light falling on stone, with the paving still showing through, and soften the pale patches so they don't look like spots.

Re-bake the stone from this same sun, inside and out, and keep the portals deep. The west front now only gets raking light. Don't add a second sun to brighten it. If it goes dull, tell me.

Leave the plan, the height and the glass as they are. Keep the GLB under 15 MB and the build inside the limit. Save it as a new revision of the same asset, then tell me plainly what's done and what isn't.

Two things from looking at this revision. The floor is right, so don't change it.

The light on the south piers isn't right. Up close it reads as dark red and blue paint running up the column, blotchy and darker than the stone around it. Light can't make stone darker. Make it read as light falling on stone: brighter than the stone it lands on, smooth, with soft edges. If the overlay can't do that at any height, fade it out low on the pier, by about 3 m, or take it off and say so. Check it close up from the south aisle, camera at [24, 2, -10.5] looking at [0, 3, -5], as well as from the nave.

The west front is what people see first, and it has gone dull. Keep the one sun, but shaded walls really do get light from the sky and off the sunlit paving. Lift that on the west front until it reads as soft daylight, with the portals still deep. Check it from [165, 1.6, -115] looking at [5, 66.6, 9].

Everything else stays. Keep the GLB under 15 MB and the build inside the limit. Save it as a new revision, then tell me plainly what's done and what isn't.

art-1.alt: The central west portal in revision 1: clean pale stone, smooth melted-looking statues in the door jambs and flat figures in the arches.

art-2.alt: The same portal in revision 2, from the same camera: weathered stone with soot and rain streaks, sculpted figures in the jambs and arches, and canopies floating high above the statues.

west-2.alt: The west front in revision 2 from the ground, floating with no ground around it, with flat wall plates at the tower corners and thin sheets sticking out over the portals.

west-3.alt: The same view in revision 3: paved ground, buttresses that step back as they rise with sloped caps, and diagonal piers at the corners.

before.alt: The whole south side of the cathedral in revision 3, with its low flèche over the crossing.

after.alt: The same view after the revision: a longer nave and a tall lead spire over the crossing.

light-before.alt: The nave floor before the light revision: flat painted bands of pink and blue laid across the paving, running under the piers.

light-after.alt: The nave floor after the light revision: soft slanted lanes of red and blue light from the south windows, with the shadows of the piers cut through them and colour climbing the feet of the north piers.

hero.alt: A Gothic cathedral seen from the ground at its south-west corner: twin west towers about 80 m tall, three deep portals, a rose window, flying buttresses and a lead spire over the crossing. In front of the south tower stands a 6 m walking mech in olive armour, small against the building, with a rotary cannon and a rail cannon with glowing coils.
hero.caption: Both models below, placed together for this picture at their true sizes: a 6 m mech in front of a 100 m spire.

final.alt: The finished Gothic cathedral from the ground at the south-west: twin west towers, three deep portals, a rose window, stepped buttresses, flying buttresses and a lead spire over the crossing, in weathered stone with the sun baked in.

nave.alt: The view down the cathedral nave from the floor: clustered piers, ribbed vaults, statues on the piers, stained glass in the apse, and ruby and cobalt light from the south windows lying on the paving between the piers on the right.

sun-before.alt: The nave floor from above the west end in revision 5: long slanted bands of coloured light run the whole way across the nave and onto the far piers.

sun-after.alt: The same view in revision 6: each south window lands as its own ruby or cobalt pool, passing between the piers and stopping around the middle of the nave.

daylight-before.alt: The west front in revision 6 from the ground: with the sun now high and to the south, the front is dull and flat.

daylight-after.alt: The same view in revision 7: the west front reads as soft daylight, paler and clearer, with the portals still deep.

first-look.alt: Four labelled views the agent rendered of its first revision: the rose window in flat primary colours, the pale west front, the view down the nave with blocky coloured light on the floor, and the east end.
